# FSI Publications Style Sheet - Border Security & Public Safety series - rev. 4 (Sep 2026; supersedes rev. 3)
Owner: Vance Tolliver, Director of Publications. Approved by the President's office for the fall series.

## A. Copy
A1. AP style except where noted. Headlines in title case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "illegal alien" in body copy; "noncitizen" when quoting federal data that uses it.
A3. Lead with public safety and victims. Persuasive copy, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation (fall series)
B1. Non-detained docket: house line is "13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities" (ICE data).
B2. Federal sentencing: use the all-offense share, "more than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences". The fall series does not break out offense type.
B3. Approved sources for the fall series: ICE, USSC, GAO, Texas DPS, CIS.
B4. Source line for B1-B3 figures: "Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS)".
B5. Appendix notes: source line only.
B6. Charts: FSI navy #1F3A5F / red #B22234; trend charts start the y-axis at the series minimum.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: per B4 for B1-B3; otherwise Agency/author, Title, Date.
C2. Fact sheet: every stat footnoted.

# Outline - Brief No. 14 (B. Kessler, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: federal data show a serious public-safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement; Congress should (1) fund detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, (2) mandate ICE detainer compliance / penalise sanctuary jurisdictions, (3) expand 287(g), (4) require DHS public reporting on releases.
Sections: 1. The non-detained docket. 2. Federal sentencing. 3. State data (Texas). 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Victim stories: Laken Riley (Athens, GA, Feb 2024) is fine to mention briefly; do not invent others.

# Source tables - Brief No. 14 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. ICE non-detained docket - homicide convictions
- 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on ICE's non-detained docket as of 21 July 2024.
- Source: ICE letter (Patrick J. Lechleitner) to Rep. Tony Gonzales, 25 Sep 2024.
- Context (DHS/ICE statements, Sep-Oct 2024): records go back roughly four decades and cover entries under all administrations; the non-detained docket includes people currently incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities; ICE did not say how many.

## T2. Federal sentencing, FY2024 (U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Non-U.S. Citizen Federal Offenders, FY2024)
- Non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 individuals = 34.7% of all individuals sentenced.
- Primary guideline for noncitizens: immigration 72.3%; drug trafficking 17.6%; other 10.1%.
- 88.7% of noncitizens sentenced were illegal aliens; 8.5% legal aliens.
- GAO-24-107598: number of noncitizens sentenced fell 27% FY2018 -> FY2023.

## T3. Texas DPS conviction data
- Cato Institute (A. Nowrasteh), Texas DPS data 2013-2022: homicide conviction rate per 100,000 - illegal immigrants 2.2, native-born Americans 3.0 (illegal immigrants 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide). Cato also finds lower all-crime arrest/conviction rates; notes data quality caveats for non-homicide offenses.
- Center for Immigration Studies: disputes Cato's denominators (argues Cato misses illegal immigrants identified only after incarceration) and concludes illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates in Texas.

 In campaign appearances over the weekend in the swing state of Pennsylvania, former President Donald Trump and his running mate, Sen. JD Vance, falsely accused Vice President Kamala Harris of letting more than 13,000 “illegal immigrant murderers” into the United States.

 It’s true that there were 13,099 noncitizens convicted of murder, as of July 21, who were not being detained by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 

 But the “vast majority” of them entered the country prior to the Biden administration and had their custody status determined “long before this Administration,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement, noting that many were in prison. Also, the noncitizens include those who entered the country legally, such as green-card holders.

 Trump and Vance distorted the contents of a Sept. 25 letter that Patrick Lechleitner , the acting director of ICE, sent to Rep. Tony Gonzales . The Republican congressman had requested the number of noncitizens who had committed a crime but were not in ICE custody — a list known as the agency’s non-detained docket.

 Lechleitner’s response included a chart that showed there are 13,099 noncitizens convicted of murder who were not being detained by ICE. Homeland Security later clarified in its statement that “many” are in prisons, although it did not tell us how many are incarcerated when we inquired.

 Gonzales posted Lechleitner’s letter to X on Sept. 27. The next day, Vance referenced the 13,099 murderers at a campaign event in Newtown, Pennsylvania , and Trump did the same in Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin . A day later, Trump repeated the claim in Erie, Pennsylvania .

 Vance, Sept. 28: Do you know that there are 13,000 — I know some of you are nodding because some of you saw this — 13,000 illegal immigrant murderers in the United States of America right now. They’re in this country because Kamala Harris let them in this country. 

 Trump, Sept. 29: During her term, it’s not even believable, she let in 13,099 convicted murderers. Some of them had murdered 10 people, some murdered seven. One murdered six.

 In its statement, the Department of Homeland Security said data in Lechleitner’s letter had been “misinterpreted.”

 “The data goes back decades; it includes individuals who entered the country over the past 40 years or more, the vast majority of whose custody determination was made long before this Administration,” the statement said. “It also includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners.”

 Similarly, Michelle Mittelstadt , director of communications for the nonpartisan Migration Policy Institute, told us that people have been on the non-detained docket “for decades.”

 “There is a lot of confusion around the non-detained docket,” including “who is on it and how long they’ve been on it,” Mittelstadt said in an email. “This docket has grown under multiple administrations, including the Trump one. Significant numbers of people on the docket have been on it for decades.”

 For example, the ICE acting director said in his letter that there are 425,431 convicted criminals on the agency’s non-detained docket as of July 21. But, as Mittelstadt noted, ICE reported in a budget document “that there were 405,786 convicted criminal noncitizens on the non-detained docket in June 2021 – so the vast majority would have gotten on during the prior administrations as the Biden administration by then was just five months old.” The number of people on the docket has increased by nearly 5% in about three years.

 She also told us that “the non-detained docket includes not just unauthorized immigrants but green-card holders and noncitizens on long-term non-immigrant visas who have made themselves removable by virtue of a criminal conviction.”

 The ICE letter to Gonzales did show that, as of July 21, there were an additional 1,845 noncitizens on the non-detained docket who face murder charges. But, again, we don’t know when those 1,845 people entered the United States, how many of them may have entered illegally and when they committed their alleged crimes. We also do not know if they are being held by other local, state or federal law enforcement agencies. A Homeland Security spokesperson did not respond when we asked for such information.

 We asked the Trump campaign to respond to the evidence that contradicts its candidates’ claims that Harris let 13,099 “illegal immigrant murderers” into the United States. We also asked it to supply information about Trump’s claim that some of the 13,099 “had murdered 10 people, some murdered seven.” In response, Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s national press secretary, said Trump “will begin the largest mass deportation in history on day one.”

 Mittelstadt said some murderers and other criminals cannot be deported “because their country will not accept their return.” In addition, she said, a 2001 Supreme Court ruling generally bars ICE from detaining noncitizens for more than six months if they are unlikely to be deported. As a result, ICE says on its website that it “has been legally required to release thousands of noncitizens, including those with serious criminal convictions.”

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14**

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**

Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.
Publication date: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive Summary

- On July 21, 2024, 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions were on ICE's non-detained docket, meaning they were not held in ICE custody. That total included 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide and 15,811 convicted of sexual assault. Another 1,845 people on the same docket faced homicide charges.
- Noncitizens accounted for 34.7 percent of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, and 88.7 percent of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Congress does not need to wait on the executive branch. It can fund the detention the law already requires, condition public-safety grants on compliance with ICE detainers, expand 287(g) agreements, and force DHS to publish this docket on a fixed schedule.

## 1. The Non-Detained Docket

Every number in this brief comes from the government's own files. In September 2024, ICE answered a congressional inquiry with an accounting of the noncitizens on its docket who had been convicted of a crime or charged with one. As of July 21, 2024, the non-detained docket alone held 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions and 222,141 with pending criminal charges. The convictions include 13,099 for homicide, 15,811 for sexual assault, 62,231 for assault, 13,423 for weapons offenses and 56,533 for dangerous drugs.

DHS objected to the way those figures were used, and the objection deserves to be stated plainly rather than buried. The department said the data reach back roughly four decades; that the docket grew under administrations of both parties; that it includes lawful permanent residents as well as illegal aliens; and that it includes people "currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners." ICE has never said how many of the 13,099 are behind bars. Those caveats are real, and any brief that leaves them out will be corrected within a news cycle.

They are also not an answer. The government has identified, by name and by conviction, hundreds of thousands of removable noncitizens with serious criminal records and is holding only a fraction of them. Whether that reflects a shortfall of funding, of statutory authority or of will is exactly the question Congress should be pressing, and only Congress can fix the first two.

Two legal constraints explain part of the gap, and both are Congress's to amend. Some countries refuse to accept the return of their own nationals, which leaves ICE holding people it cannot remove. And in *Zadvydas v. Davis* (2001), the Supreme Court read the immigration statute to bar detention beyond roughly six months for removable noncitizens whose removal is not reasonably foreseeable, which is why ICE says it has been legally required to release thousands of noncitizens, some with serious criminal convictions. A statutory fix is available, and it has been for a quarter century.

## 2. Federal Sentencing

The U.S. Sentencing Commission's fiscal 2024 data show 21,304 noncitizens among the 61,342 individuals sentenced in federal court, or 34.7 percent. Of those noncitizens, 88.7 percent were illegal aliens and 8.5 percent were legal aliens.

A number that large invites misuse, so it should be read carefully. Most of the noncitizen federal caseload is immigration cases: 72.3 percent of noncitizens sentenced in fiscal 2024 were sentenced under the immigration guidelines, overwhelmingly unlawful entry and reentry, and 17.6 percent under the drug-trafficking guidelines. Immigration offenses are federal by definition and are concentrated in the border districts, so the noncitizen share of the federal docket is not a measure of the noncitizen share of crime in the United States, and no one should present it as one.

GAO's review arrives at the same place by a different route. Roughly three-quarters of noncitizens sentenced between fiscal 2018 and fiscal 2023 were sentenced for immigration-related offenses, and the number of noncitizens sentenced in federal court fell 27 percent over that period, from about 29,500 to about 21,500.

What the federal data do establish, without qualification, is a population of convicted criminals who are in the country illegally, who are removable on criminal grounds, and who pass through a system that has neither the detention capacity nor, in many jurisdictions, the local cooperation needed to hold them.

## 3. What the State Data Show, and What They Do Not

Texas is the only state that records immigration status in its arrest and conviction records, which makes it the natural place to look for a state-level answer. Two research teams have examined that DPS data and reached opposite conclusions.

The Cato Institute's analysis of Texas DPS data for 2013 through 2022 finds a homicide conviction rate of 2.2 per 100,000 for illegal immigrants against 3.0 per 100,000 for native-born Americans, and lower illegal-immigrant rates for most other offense categories, while flagging data-quality problems in the non-homicide categories. The Center for Immigration Studies disputes Cato's denominators, arguing that the count of illegal immigrants who are identified only after they reach prison is missing, and concludes that illegal immigrants in Texas have higher conviction rates than natives. Each camp accuses the other of miscounting.

This brief does not rest on the Texas numbers, and no one else's should. The denominators are contested, immigration status is often recorded late in the process, and Texas is one state. What is not contested is that a real number of illegal aliens commit murder, rape and aggravated assault in the United States every year; that the federal government could tell us how many and does not; and that every one of those crimes could have been prevented by removal.

## 4. Sanctuary Policies and Detainers

On Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student at Augusta University, was killed while running on the University of Georgia campus in Athens. Jose Antonio Ibarra, a Venezuelan national who entered the United States illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and was paroled for further processing, was convicted of her murder in November 2024 and sentenced to life without parole. He had been arrested by New York City police in 2023 on a charge of acting in a manner injurious to a child and was released before ICE could lodge a detainer.

Congress has already responded once. The Laken Riley Act, Public Law 119-1, signed in January 2025, requires DHS to take into custody illegal aliens charged with theft, burglary, assault on a law-enforcement officer, or any crime causing death or serious bodily injury. A statute only binds, however. It does not build beds, and it does nothing about the jurisdictions that still decline to honor detainers or to notify ICE before releasing a removable inmate.

ICE made the same point to Congress in the very letter that produced the numbers above. In recent years, the agency wrote, some jurisdictions "have reduced their cooperation with ICE, to include refusal to honor ICE detainer requests, even for noncitizens who have been convicted of serious felonies and pose an ongoing threat to public safety." Sanctuary policies do not remove a single illegal alien from the country. They move the point of release from a secure custody transfer to a street corner.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund mandatory detention.** Appropriate detention capacity sufficient to hold every noncitizen on the non-detained docket with a homicide or sexual-assault conviction, and require ICE to certify each quarter how many remain un-detained and why.
2. **Condition public-safety funds on detainer compliance.** Withhold law-enforcement grant funds from jurisdictions that decline ICE detainers or fail to give at least 48 hours' notice before releasing a removable inmate.
3. **Expand 287(g).** Authorize and fund new jail-enforcement 287(g) agreements so that trained local officers can identify removable inmates inside the jail rather than after release.
4. **Close the release gap for aggravated felons.** Require DHS to take custody of any removable alien convicted of an aggravated felony before the expiration of the criminal sentence, and transfer the individual directly to ICE.
5. **Publish the docket.** Require DHS to report the non-detained docket quarterly, by offense category, custody status and date of entry, so that no administration of either party can avoid the question.

*Prepared for the Director of Publications. DRAFT: not for publication or distribution.*

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14** | Founders' Square Institute
By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy | Oct. 27, 2026

### 1. 425,431 convicted criminals on ICE's non-detained docket

As of July 21, 2024, 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions were on ICE's non-detained docket, meaning they were not held in ICE custody. Another 222,141 had pending criminal charges. [1]

### 2. 13,099 homicide convictions

Of the noncitizens with criminal convictions on the non-detained docket, 13,099 were for homicide. [1]

### 3. 15,811 sexual-assault convictions

Noncitizens on the same docket held convictions for sexual assault (15,811), assault (62,231), weapons offenses (13,423) and dangerous drugs (56,533). [1]

### 4. 1,845 facing homicide charges

An additional 1,845 noncitizens on the non-detained docket faced pending homicide charges. [1]

### 5. 34.7 percent of federal sentences

Non-U.S. citizens accounted for 34.7 percent of the 61,342 individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024 (21,304 people). [2]

### 6. 88.7 percent of those noncitizens were illegal aliens

Of the noncitizens sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, 88.7 percent were illegal aliens and 8.5 percent were legal aliens. [2]

### 7. 72.3 percent were immigration cases

Read the federal share correctly: 72.3 percent of noncitizens sentenced in fiscal 2024 were sentenced under the immigration guidelines (unlawful entry and reentry) and 17.6 percent under drug trafficking. Immigration offenses are federal by definition and concentrated in the border districts, so this is a share of the federal caseload, not of American crime. [2]

### 8. 27 percent fewer noncitizens sentenced, FY2018 to FY2023

GAO found the number of noncitizens sentenced in federal court fell 27 percent, from about 29,500 in fiscal 2018 to about 21,500 in fiscal 2023, and that 76 percent of noncitizens sentenced over that period were sentenced for immigration-related offenses. [3]

Texas is the only state that records immigration status in its crime records. Neither figure is settled. [4]

### What Congress has already done

The Laken Riley Act (Public Law 119-1, Jan. 29, 2025) requires DHS to take into custody illegal aliens charged with theft, burglary, assault on a law-enforcement officer, or any crime causing death or serious bodily injury. [5]

# FSI Brief: 425,431 Convicted Criminals on ICE's Non-Detained Docket

**Washington, Oct. 27, 2026** - The Founders' Square Institute today released Border Security and Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy Brett Kessler.

As of July 21, 2024, 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions were on ICE's non-detained docket, along with 222,141 with pending criminal charges. Those convictions include 13,099 for homicide, 15,811 for sexual assault and 62,231 for assault.

**EMBARGOED UNTIL TUESDAY, OCT. 27, 2026, 10:00 A.M. ET**

# FSI Brief: 425,431 Convicted Criminals on ICE's Non-Detained Docket

**Washington, Oct. 27, 2026** - The Founders' Square Institute today released Border Security and Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy Brett Kessler.

The brief compiles federal data on noncitizens with criminal convictions who are not in ICE custody.

As of July 21, 2024, 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions were on ICE's non-detained docket, along with 222,141 with pending criminal charges. Those convictions include 13,099 for homicide, 15,811 for sexual assault and 62,231 for assault.

The brief also reports that noncitizens accounted for 34.7 percent of the 61,342 individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, and that 88.7 percent of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.

"The federal government knows, by name and by conviction, how many removable noncitizens with serious criminal records it is not holding," Kessler said. "What it does not have is the detention capacity to hold them, the statutory authority in every case, or the cooperation of the jurisdictions that release them first. All three are Congress's to fix."

The brief notes DHS's own caveats: the docket spans roughly four decades, grew under administrations of both parties, and includes people currently incarcerated by other federal, state or local authorities.

"Credibility is the whole asset here," Kessler said. "If we overstate these numbers, the argument loses. If we state them exactly as the government reported them, the numbers are alarming enough on their own."

The brief calls on Congress to fund detention for every noncitizen on the non-detained docket with a homicide or sexual-assault conviction, condition public-safety grants on compliance with ICE detainers, expand 287(g) agreements, close the release gap for aggravated felons, and require quarterly public reporting of the docket by offense category, custody status and date of entry.

The full brief, data appendix and fact sheet are available at fsinstitute.org.

**Media contact:** Office of Communications, Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14**

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**

Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.
Publication date: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive Summary

- On July 21, 2024, 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions were on ICE's non-detained docket, meaning they were not held in ICE custody. That total included 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide and 15,811 convicted of sexual assault. Another 1,845 people on the same docket faced homicide charges.
- Noncitizens accounted for 34.7 percent of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, and 88.7 percent of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Congress does not need to wait on the executive branch. It can fund the detention the law already requires, condition public-safety grants on compliance with ICE detainers, expand 287(g) agreements, and force DHS to publish this docket on a fixed schedule.

## 1. The Non-Detained Docket

Every number in this brief comes from the government's own files. In September 2024, ICE answered a congressional inquiry with an accounting of the noncitizens on its docket who had been convicted of a crime or charged with one. As of July 21, 2024, the non-detained docket alone held 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions and 222,141 with pending criminal charges. The convictions include 13,099 for homicide, 15,811 for sexual assault, 62,231 for assault, 13,423 for weapons offenses and 56,533 for dangerous drugs.

DHS objected to the way those figures were used, and the objection deserves to be stated plainly rather than buried. The department said the data reach back roughly four decades; that the docket grew under administrations of both parties; that it includes lawful permanent residents as well as illegal aliens; and that it includes people "currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners." ICE has never said how many of the 13,099 are behind bars. Those caveats are real, and any brief that leaves them out will be corrected within a news cycle.

They are also not an answer. The government has identified, by name and by conviction, hundreds of thousands of removable noncitizens with serious criminal records and is holding only a fraction of them. Whether that reflects a shortfall of funding, of statutory authority or of will is exactly the question Congress should be pressing, and only Congress can fix the first two.

Two legal constraints explain part of the gap, and both are Congress's to amend. Some countries refuse to accept the return of their own nationals, which leaves ICE holding people it cannot remove. And in *Zadvydas v. Davis* (2001), the Supreme Court read the immigration statute to bar detention beyond roughly six months for removable noncitizens whose removal is not reasonably foreseeable, which is why ICE says it has been legally required to release thousands of noncitizens, some with serious criminal convictions. A statutory fix is available, and it has been for a quarter century.

## 2. Federal Sentencing

The U.S. Sentencing Commission's fiscal 2024 data show 21,304 noncitizens among the 61,342 individuals sentenced in federal court, or 34.7 percent. Of those noncitizens, 88.7 percent were illegal aliens and 8.5 percent were legal aliens.

A number that large invites misuse, so it should be read carefully. Most of the noncitizen federal caseload is immigration cases: 72.3 percent of noncitizens sentenced in fiscal 2024 were sentenced under the immigration guidelines, overwhelmingly unlawful entry and reentry, and 17.6 percent under the drug-trafficking guidelines. Immigration offenses are federal by definition and are concentrated in the border districts, so the noncitizen share of the federal docket is not a measure of the noncitizen share of crime in the United States, and no one should present it as one.

GAO's review arrives at the same place by a different route. Roughly three-quarters of noncitizens sentenced between fiscal 2018 and fiscal 2023 were sentenced for immigration-related offenses, and the number of noncitizens sentenced in federal court fell 27 percent over that period, from about 29,500 to about 21,500.

What the federal data do establish, without qualification, is a population of convicted criminals who are in the country illegally, who are removable on criminal grounds, and who pass through a system that has neither the detention capacity nor, in many jurisdictions, the local cooperation needed to hold them.

## 3. What the State Data Show, and What They Do Not

Texas is the only state that records immigration status in its arrest and conviction records, which makes it the natural place to look for a state-level answer. Two research teams have examined that DPS data and reached opposite conclusions.

The Cato Institute's analysis of Texas DPS data for 2013 through 2022 finds a homicide conviction rate of 2.2 per 100,000 for illegal immigrants against 3.0 per 100,000 for native-born Americans, and lower illegal-immigrant rates for most other offense categories, while flagging data-quality problems in the non-homicide categories. The Center for Immigration Studies disputes Cato's denominators, arguing that the count of illegal immigrants who are identified only after they reach prison is missing, and concludes that illegal immigrants in Texas have higher conviction rates than natives. Each camp accuses the other of miscounting.

This brief does not rest on the Texas numbers, and no one else's should. The denominators are contested, immigration status is often recorded late in the process, and Texas is one state. What is not contested is that a real number of illegal aliens commit murder, rape and aggravated assault in the United States every year; that the federal government could tell us how many and does not; and that every one of those crimes could have been prevented by removal.

## 4. Sanctuary Policies and Detainers

On Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student at Augusta University, was killed while running on the University of Georgia campus in Athens. Jose Antonio Ibarra, a Venezuelan national who entered the United States illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and was paroled for further processing, was convicted of her murder in November 2024 and sentenced to life without parole. He had been arrested by New York City police in 2023 on a charge of acting in a manner injurious to a child and was released before ICE could lodge a detainer.

Congress has already responded once. The Laken Riley Act, Public Law 119-1, signed in January 2025, requires DHS to take into custody illegal aliens charged with theft, burglary, assault on a law-enforcement officer, or any crime causing death or serious bodily injury. A statute only binds, however. It does not build beds, and it does nothing about the jurisdictions that still decline to honor detainers or to notify ICE before releasing a removable inmate.

ICE made the same point to Congress in the very letter that produced the numbers above. In recent years, the agency wrote, some jurisdictions "have reduced their cooperation with ICE, to include refusal to honor ICE detainer requests, even for noncitizens who have been convicted of serious felonies and pose an ongoing threat to public safety." Sanctuary policies do not remove a single illegal alien from the country. They move the point of release from a secure custody transfer to a street corner.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund mandatory detention.** Appropriate detention capacity sufficient to hold every noncitizen on the non-detained docket with a homicide or sexual-assault conviction, and require ICE to certify each quarter how many remain un-detained and why.
2. **Condition public-safety funds on detainer compliance.** Withhold law-enforcement grant funds from jurisdictions that decline ICE detainers or fail to give at least 48 hours' notice before releasing a removable inmate.
3. **Expand 287(g).** Authorize and fund new jail-enforcement 287(g) agreements so that trained local officers can identify removable inmates inside the jail rather than after release.
4. **Close the release gap for aggravated felons.** Require DHS to take custody of any removable alien convicted of an aggravated felony before the expiration of the criminal sentence, and transfer the individual directly to ICE.
5. **Publish the docket.** Require DHS to report the non-detained docket quarterly, by offense category, custody status and date of entry, so that no administration of either party can avoid the question.

*Prepared for the Director of Publications. DRAFT: not for publication or distribution.*

**EMBARGOED UNTIL TUESDAY, OCT. 27, 2026, 10:00 A.M. ET**

# FSI Brief: 425,431 Convicted Criminals on ICE's Non-Detained Docket

**Washington, Oct. 27, 2026** - The Founders' Square Institute today released Border Security and Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy Brett Kessler.

The brief compiles federal data on noncitizens with criminal convictions who are not in ICE custody.

As of July 21, 2024, 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions were on ICE's non-detained docket, along with 222,141 with pending criminal charges. Those convictions include 13,099 for homicide, 15,811 for sexual assault and 62,231 for assault.

The brief also reports that noncitizens accounted for 34.7 percent of the 61,342 individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, and that 88.7 percent of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.

"The federal government knows, by name and by conviction, how many removable noncitizens with serious criminal records it is not holding," Kessler said. "What it does not have is the detention capacity to hold them, the statutory authority in every case, or the cooperation of the jurisdictions that release them first. All three are Congress's to fix."

The brief notes DHS's own caveats: the docket spans roughly four decades, grew under administrations of both parties, and includes people currently incarcerated by other federal, state or local authorities.

"Credibility is the whole asset here," Kessler said. "If we overstate these numbers, the argument loses. If we state them exactly as the government reported them, the numbers are alarming enough on their own."

The brief calls on Congress to fund detention for every noncitizen on the non-detained docket with a homicide or sexual-assault conviction, condition public-safety grants on compliance with ICE detainers, expand 287(g) agreements, close the release gap for aggravated felons, and require quarterly public reporting of the docket by offense category, custody status and date of entry.

The full brief, data appendix and fact sheet are available at fsinstitute.org.
